## Methods

Cell culture and drug treatments
HCT116 cells CCL247 are from ATCC source, HeLa H9 cells were a gift from E. Emiliani and HeLa Kyoto a gift from I. Poser69. HCT116 cells and HeLa cells were grown in McCoy’s 5A medium (Gibco) or Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s Medium DMEM (Gibco), respectively, containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Sigma-Aldrich) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) at 37°C, 5% CO2. All cells were routinely tested for the absence of mycoplasma. For cell treatments, drugs were used as follows: puromycin at 100 µg/mL for 30 min (Invivogen), CB-6644 at 500 nM for 4 to 16 h (MedChemExpress), geldanamycin at 2 µM for 1 h (Invivogen), cycloheximide at 200 µg/mL for 20 min (Thermo Scientific), and harringtonine at 3 µg/mL for 30 min (MedChemExpress).

Cloning, plasmids and transfection
Plasmids were constructed using the Gateway technology (Invitrogen) with donor vectors from the human ORFeome70. Detailed maps are available upon request. DsRed2-DDX6fm was designed and used as described before14. Stable cell lines expressing DsRed2-DDX6fm-RUVBL1 or DsRed2-DDX6fm-RPAP3 were obtained using the Flp-In system (Thermo-Fischer Scientific) with hygromycin selection (50 mg/mL). Transient transfection was performed for the DsRed2-DDX6fm-KPNA3 construct. All transfections were performed using JetPrime according to the manufacturer's instructions: 200 µL JetPrime Buffer (Polyplus), 2 µg vector DNA, and 4 µL Jetprime reagent (Polyplus) for cells cultured in 2 mL in 6-well plates. Unless indicated otherwise, oligos were provided by Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT).

Generation of stable cell lines using PiggyBac transposon system
POLR2A and EFTUD2 cDNA WT or containing a STOP were fused at the C-terminus of a mCherry tag in the pDest-PiggyBac vector under the control of the UbC promoter. The constructs were transfected in the HCT116-RUVBL1-GFP cell line. 0.3 µg of each plasmid, alongside 1.7 µg of a construct expressing the transposase71 were transfected overnight with JetPrime (Polyplus). The day after, the transfection medium was replaced by fresh medium. Cells positively expressing mCherry were sorted using Melody FACS. mCherry-POLR2A protein expression and localization were further verified by fluorescent microscopy and Western blots.

Insertion of GFP and SunTag cassettes by CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in
HCT116 cells were CRISPR/Cas9 edited to insert an mAID-GFP-IRES-Neomycin cassette in fusion to the C-termini of RPAP3 and RUVBL1. The recombination cassettes contained 500 bases of homology arms flanking a cassette composed of mAID-GFP, a stop codon, an IRES containing a start codon fused to a Neomycin resistance gene, and a stop codon. HeLa Flp-In cells stably expressing the SunTag scFv-sfGFP were CRISPR/Cas9 edited to insert a SunTag*32 cassette at the C-terminus of RPAP3. Cells were selected on 800 µg/mL G418 neomycin for a few weeks. Individual clones were then picked and analyzed for GFP expression by fluorescence microscopy, Western blotting and PCR genotyping. The sequences targeted by the guide RNAs were (PAM sequences are lowercase): TCAGCAGTAAGAGACTCCCCagg for RUVBL1 guide 1, ACTTCATGTACTTATCCTGCtgg for RUVBL1 guide 2; GAGCTGAAAAAGAGGTATGGtgg for the RPAP3 guide. PCR genotyping was conducted using Phusion polymerase (New England Biolabs) and genomic DNA prepared with Wizard® Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega). The sequences of the oligonucleotides were as follows (5’ to 3’): Fw1 in the gene before the homology arms: GGTGAAGTCCCCATGTCCTG for RUVBL1 and TGTCGACCGATCAGTGGTAGTAA for RPAP3; Rev1 in the mAID-GFP cassette: CGGTGCTCCGTCCATTGATA; Rev2 in the SunTag*32 cassette: ACTAGTGACCGGTCCTCTAGA; Fw2 in the repair cassettes: GTTCATAAACGCGGGGTTCG; Rev2 in the gene after the homology arm: CGCAGCTCTCATCCTACTGG for RUVBL1 and ACGCTACACTCACATCCAACA for RPAP3.

Western blots
Proteins were resuspended in Laemmli 1X, boiled for 5 min, separated by 10% SDS-PAGE, and transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane (Protran). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk (weight/volume) in TBST (TBS with 0.5% Tween-20) and incubated in 1% non-fat milk in TBST with the primary antibodies overnight at 4°C followed by three times 5 min washes in TBST at RT, and incubation with secondary antibodies conjugated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP) for 1 h at RT, and finally washed three times 10 min in TBST at RT. Enzymatic activity was detected using the SuperSignal West Pico/Femto Chemiluminescent Substrate (Genetex) or Immobilon (Roche). The primary antibodies used were: anti-RPAP3 (Sigma SAB1411438-100UG, 1/1000 dilution), anti-RUVBL1 (Proteintech 10210-2-AP, 1/500 dilution), anti-GAPDH (Abcam 8245, 1/20000 dilution), anti-GFP (Roche 11814460001, 1/1000 dilution), anti-mCherry (abcam ab213511, 1/1000), anti-BRD8 (Proteintech 10476-1-AP, 1/1000 dilution). Secondary antibodies were anti-rabbit (Abcam ab6721, dilution 1/10000) and anti-mouse (Abcam ab6728, dilution 1/5000) coupled to HRP.

Immunofluorescence
2.105 to 3.105 cells were grown on Ø12 mm glass coverslips, treated as indicated and after 48 h washed with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT then washed with PBS. Permeabilization was done in 0.1% Triton X-100 (Thermo-scientific) in PBS for 10 min at RT. After 3 PBS washes, coverslips were incubated in PBS/BSA 1% or PBS/FBS 1% with primary antibodies for 1 h at RT, washed three times in PBS, incubated with secondary antibody for 1 h at RT, and washed three times again in PBS. Primary antibodies used were anti-POLR2A (PB-7C2, Euromedex, 1/100 dilution), anti-RPAP3 (Sigma SAB1411438-100UG, 1/100 dilution), anti-HUR (Santa Cruz Biotechnology sc-5261, 1/100 dilution) and anti-HSP90α/β (Santa Cruz Biotechnology sc-13119, 1/100 dilution) and anti-p70S6 Kinase (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-8418, 1/100 dilution). Secondary antibodies were: anti-mouse Cy3 diluted 1/1000 (#115-165-003); anti-rabbit Cy3 diluted 1/1000 (#711-166-152); anti-mouse FITC diluted 1/200 (#115-546-006); anti-rabbit FITC diluted 1/200 (#111-096-047) anti-mouse Cy5 diluted 1/200 (#115-176-003) and anti-rabbit Cy5 diluted 1/200 (#111-175-144). Coverslips were mounted in Vectashield medium containing DAPI (Vector Laboratories).

Single molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH) with DNA probes
Cells were grown on glass coverslips or glass-bottom 96-well plates (Greiner 655892), fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT and permeabilized with 70% ethanol overnight at 4°C. To detect a specific mRNA, 24–48 unlabeled primary DNA probes complementary to the RNA of interest were used (Supplementary Data 3). In addition to hybridizing to their targets, these probes contained a FLAP sequence that was pre-hybridized to a complementary secondary probe coupled to a fluorophore, as described previously71. Pre-hybridization was done in NEBuffer 3 (NEB, 10 mM NaCl, 5 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM MgCl2, pH 7.9) according to the ratios indicated in Supplementary Data 3 and using a thermocycler with the following program: 85°C for 3 min, 65°C for 3 min, and 25°C for 5 min. Cells on coverslips were first incubated in 1x SSC, 5 M urea (Sigma-Aldrich) for 15 min at RT, and then incubated with the hybridization mixture containing the probe duplexes (2 µl of pre-hybridization mix per 100 µl of final volume), with 1X SSC, 0.34 mg/mL tRNA, 5 M urea, 2 mM VRC, 0.2 mg/mL RNAse-free BSA, 10% Dextran sulfate, overnight in a wet chamber at 37°C. The day after, the samples were washed three times for 30 min in the wash buffer (1x SSC, 5 M urea) at 37°C and rinsed twice in PBS at RT. The 96-plates were incubated in the dark with 5 µg/mL DAPI for 40 min at RT, then mounted in Vectashield medium without DAPI (Vector Laboratories, Inc.).

SmFISH in 96-well plates with RNA probes
Cells were grown in a 96-well plate with glass bottom (Greiner 655892), fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS at RT for 20 min and permeabilized with 70% ethanol overnight at 4°C. Probe sets of DNA oligonucleotides (GenScript) targeting the mRNAs of interest were generated based on the Oligostan script72. Each oligo is composed of a specific hybridization sequence flanked by 2 readout sequences and a barcode shared among the gene probeset (Supplementary Data 3). Gene-specific probes were amplified by PCR with the gene-specific barcodes before being transcribed in vitro to obtain transcript-specific primary RNA probe sets, as described previously73. For each mRNA of interest, 50 ng of primary RNA probes and 25 ng of each fluorescent secondary DNA probes (TYE-650-labeled LNA/DNA oligonucleotides, Qiagen)73 targeting the readout sequences were pre-hybridized in 100 µl of a solution containing 7.5 M urea (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.34 mg/ml tRNA (Sigma-Aldrich) and 10% Dextran sulfate. Pre-hybridization was performed in a thermocycler, with the following program: 90°C for 3 min, 53°C for 15 min. Cells in 96-well plates were washed with PBS and incubated for 15 min at RT in hybridization buffer (1X SSC, 7.5 M urea) before adding 100 µL of the hybridization mixture to each well. Hybridization was performed at 48°C overnight. The next day, the plate was washed 8 times for 20 min each in 1X SSC, and 7.5 M urea at 48°C. Finally, cells were washed twice with PBS at RT for 10 min each, stained with 5 µg/mL DAPI, and mounted in 90% glycerol (VWR), 1 mg/mL p-Phenylenediamine (Sigma-Aldrich), in PBS pH 8.

Image acquisition
Coverslip images were acquired using a 63x oil immersion objective (1.4 NA, PL Apo, oil) on a Leica DM6B microscope. DAPI, GFP, CY3, and CY5 channels were imaged using the following filter combinations: 405/60, 455, 470/40; 470/40, 495, 525/50; 545/30, 570, 610/75; 620/60, 660, 700/75. Alternatively, coverslips were imaged using a 63X objective (Plan Apochromat, 1.4 NA, oil) on a Zeiss Axioimager Z2 widefield microscope. DAPI, GFP, CY3, and CY5 channels were then imaged using the following filter combinations: <365, FT 395, 445/50; 470/40, FT 495, 525/50; 545/25, 570, 605/70; 610/30, 660, 640/50. Images were taken as Z-stacks with one plane every 0.24 µm (Zeiss Z2) or every 0.376 µm (Leica Thunder). 96-well plates were imaged on an Opera Phenix High-Content Screening System (PerkinElmer), with a 63× water-immersion objective (NA 1.15). Three-dimensional images were acquired, consisting of 18 slices with a spacing of 0.6 µm. RPS6 and HSP90 staining were acquired using a Zeiss LSM980 Airyscan confocal microscope equipped with a 63X Plan Apo oil 1.4 NA objective.

Image analysis
Image quantifications were based on an image analysis pipeline that included cell segmentation, threshold-based spot detection, dense region deconvolution, and a Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm. Firstly, nuclei and cytoplasm segmentation were inferred in 2D on image stack mean projection using Cellpose neural network74. Secondly, single molecules were detected as 3D spots using the Big-FISH package75, which relies on an intensity Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) filter followed by a local maxima filter and a user-adjusted threshold. During analysis, we ensured that the same thresholds were applied to images made for the same RNA, for all cell treatments. As local maxima detection can lead to a misestimation of single molecule number in bright regions where individual molecules cannot be distinguished, a dense region deconvolution step was added. It consists of fitting the median detected spot with a 3D-gaussian to construct a reference spot and then reconstructing the bright region signal using multiple reference spots, thus providing the number of single RNAs in bright regions. Thirdly, a DBSCAN was used to assign spots to clusters (foci). At this point, detected spots were divided in clustered spots (spots assigned to a cluster) or free spots. Finally, a centroid calculation was performed to assign coordinates to each cluster. This single-molecule quantification process was repeated on all smFISH or SunTag channels, enabling quantification of RNA colocalization. During analysis, filtering was used to discard aberrations: (i) cells without nucleus or with more than one nuclei; (ii) any cell whose mask laid on the border of the field of view and that was thus considered incomplete; (iii) any spot detected outside of segmented cells; (iv) any regions containing an abnormally high average of 2 spots per pixel in a sphere of 1400 nm. Distances between spots were computed using the exact Euclidian distance. Finally, spots were considered colocalizing when found closer together than a cutoff distance of 310 nm.

A pipeline named SmallFish was also developed to quantify single mRNAs and clusters, and evaluate the percentage of colocalization between clusters. It provides a ready-to-use graphical interface to combine the Python packages used for cell analysis. In the pipeline, cell segmentation (2D) was performed using Cellpose (https://github.com/MouseLand/cellpose), while spot detection was carried out using BigFish (https://github.com/fish-quant/big-fish). Clusters were considered colocalizing when found closer together than a cutoff distance of 310 nm. Boxplots graphs were constructed on Python using Seaborn package76 and Statannotations package77.

RNA immunoprecipitation for RIP-seq
HCT116 cells with GFP-tagged RUVBL1 or RPAP3 alleles were seeded in 15 cm plates (1 plate/condition). At 70% confluency, cells were left untreated or treated as follows: with puromycin for 30 min at 100 µg/mL; with CB-6644 for 16 h at 500 nM; with both CB-6644 for 16 h and puromycin for 30 min. All treatments were done at 37°C. After treatments, cells were put on ice and washed twice with ice-cold PBS and then lysed with 0.5 mL HNTG lysis buffer (20 mM Hepes pH 7.9, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 10% glycerol, 1 mM MgCl2, and 1 mM EGTA) supplemented with a cocktail of protease inhibitors (Roche). Cells were incubated for 30 min on a tube roller at 4°C before being centrifuged for 10 min at 16,000×g at 4°C. The supernatant was subjected to immunoprecipitation for 1.5 h at 4°C using GFP-Trap agarose beads (Chromotek-gta-20). Agarose control beads (Chromotek-bab-20) were used for non-specific control IP. All experiments were done in duplicates. Beads were washed 5 times with ice-cold HNTG. RNeasy minikit (Qiagen-74106) was used to purify RNAs. DNA contamination was eliminated by a TURBO-DNA Free kit, as recommended by the manufacturer (Invitrogen-AM1907).

RNA-sequencing and analysis
SMART-Seq Stranded Kit (Takara Bio) was used to generate cDNA libraries for high-throughput sequencing using NovaSeq 6000 Illumina. RNA and DNA libraries' quality was subjected to quality control checks periodically (or after each step) using a fragment analyzer (Kit high sensitivity NGS) and qPCR (Roche LightCycler 480). Ribosomal cDNAs were cleaved with scZapR enzyme in the presence of scRProbes designed against mammalian ribosomal RNAs. Libraries were then sequenced with NovaSeq Reagent Kits on a flow cell SP (single read, −100 nucleotides) using the 2-channel sequence-by-synthesis method. Before demultiplexing, sequences were mixed with PhiX sequences as an Illumina control (not indexed). Demultiplexing was realized using Illumina bcl2fastq software (v2.20.0.422), and all PhiX sequences were removed.

FastaQC software (v0.11.9) provided a tool to check read quality after high-throughput sequencing, and the MultiQC program (V1.12) served to group data that emerges from all samples. FastQ screen software served to detect contaminating genomes. Sequences were aligned on 15 species genomes, mycoplasma, and ribosomal RNAs using Bowtie2 software. No contamination was detected.

TopHat2 software (v2.1.1) was used to align the obtained reads on the human genome (hg38 version) and to annotate them according to NBCI database. FeatureCounts software was utilized to count reads per gene. All reads that overlap on two genes or show alignment at different positions on the genome were discarded. Counts were normalized in each sample to eliminated differences due to manipulation. This was done by a normalization method known as relative log expression (RLE). Differential expression genes were identified using EdgeR (v3.34.1). Tests are based on a generalized linear model and allow count modeling using a negative binomial distribution. To calculate the reads per kilobase per million mapped reads (RPKM), the formula below was used: (read counts aligned on a specific gene / (total aligned counts x gene length) x 109.

Label-free quantitative proteomics
HCT116 cells with RUVBL1 or RPAP3 endogenously tagged with GFP were seeded in 15 cm plates (1 plate/condition). At 70% confluency, cells were treated or not with CB-6644 for 16 h at 500 nM. Cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, then lysed with 0.5 mL HNTG lysis buffer supplemented with proteinase inhibitor cocktail (Roche; see above for the composition of HNTG). Cells were scraped and incubated for 15 min at 4°C before being centrifuged for 10 min at 16,000×g at 4°C. The supernatant was subjected to immunoprecipitation using GFP-Trap agarose beads (Chromotek-gta-20). Agarose control beads (Chromotek-bab-20) were used for non-specific control IP. All experiments were done in triplicates. Extracts were incubated with beads for 1.5 h at 4°C and washed 5 times with ice-cold HNTG. Proteins were then eluted in Laemmli buffer and heated for 10 min at 95°C.

For sample digestion, proteins were loaded onto SDS-PAGE (10% polyacrylamide, Mini-PROTEAN® TGX™ Precast Gels, Bio-Rad) and stained with Protein Staining Solution (Euromedex). Gel lanes were cut into one single band and destained with 50 mM TriEthylAmmonium BiCarbonate (TEABC, Merck), followed by three washes in 100% acetonitrile. After reduction (with 10 mM dithiothreitol in 50 mM TEABC at 60°C for 30 min) and alkylation (with 55 mM iodoacetamide in 50 mM TEABC at room temperature for 30 min), proteins were digested in-gel using trypsin (1 g/band, Gold, Promega). Digest products were vacuum-dried before LC-MS/MS analysis. For mass spectrometry, a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with an Ultimate 3000 nano-HPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used. Peptide samples were solubilized in 0.05% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) / 2% ACN, and were injected for desalting and pre-concentration on a PepMap® 100 C18 precolumn (0.3 mm x 5 mm; ThermoFisher Scientific). Peptides separation were done on a 50 cm analytical reversed-phase column (75 mm inner diameter, Acclaim Pepmap 100® C18, ThermoFisher Scientific) using a 120 min gradient of 2 to 40% of buffer B (80% ACN, 0.1% formic acid) and a flow rate of 300 nL/min. MS/MS analyses were performed in a data-dependent mode. Full scans (375-1500 m/z) were acquired on the Orbitrap mass analyzer with a 60,000 resolution at 200 m/z. For the full scans, 3e6 ions were accumulated within a maximum injection time of 60 ms and detected in the Orbitrap analyzer. The twelve most intense ions with charge states ≥2 were sequentially isolated to a target value of 1e5 with a maximum injection time of 100 ms and fragmented by HCD (Higher-energy collisional dissociation) in the collision cell (normalized collision energy of 28%) and detected in the Orbitrap analyzer at 30,000 resolution. First mass was set to 100 m/z.

Raw spectra were processed using the MaxQuant environment (v.2.0.3.0), and Andromeda for database search with label-free quantification (LFQ), match between runs, and the iBAQ algorithm (CIT)78. The MS/MS spectra were matched against the UniProt Reference proteome of Homo sapiens (Proteome ID UP000005640; release 2022_03; https://www.uniprot.org/) and a homemade contaminant database. Different release versions were used, depending on the date of analysis. Enzyme specificity was set to trypsin/P, and the search included cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification and oxidation of methionine, and acetylation (protein N-term) as variable modifications. Up to two missed cleavages were allowed for protease digestion. FDR was set at 0.01 for peptides and proteins and the minimal peptide length at 7. A representative protein ID in each protein group was automatically selected using an in-house developed bioinformatic tool (Leading tool 3.4) as the best annotated protein in UniProtKB (reviewed entries rather than automatic ones79. Analysis of quantification data, statistical analyses and graphical representations were performed using Perseus (v1.6.15). Briefly, label-free quantification (LFQ) intensity-based values were log2 transformed. Imputation of missing values was performed using Perseus with standard parameters (normal distribution, width = 0.3, shift = 1.8). Normalized LFQ intensities were compared between replicates, using a 1% permutation-based false discovery rate (FDR) in a two-tailed Student’s t test (250 randomizations)80.

RT-qPCR
RNA immunoprecipitation was performed as described before except that DNAse Treatment was neglected. The reverse transcription reaction (RT) was carried out by mixing 2 µL of RNA with final 2.5 µM of random primers (Thermofisher Scientific) and 0.5 mM of dNTP mix (Thermofisher Scientific). The RNA-primers mix was incubated for 5 min at 65°C then for 1 min on ice. 100 U of SuperScript IV enzyme was added to the mix in addition to a final 1X SuperScript Buffer, 5 mM DTT (Thermofisher Scientific) and 20 U of the RNase Out recombinant RNase inhibitor (Invitrogen). The final mix (Vf = 20 µL) was incubated for 10 min at 23°C, 10 min at 50°C followed by 10 min at 80°C to inactivate the enzyme. The RT reaction was then diluted 4x by adding 60 µL of RNAse Free H2O.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors explore an important area in protein translation and folding: how do protein complexes assemble? There is a lot of conjecture within the field regarding whether such assembly can occur during translation, and if so, by what mechanism. In this work, the authors have studied R2TP, a HSP90 co-chaperone using a range of cell-based assays (including proteomics, smFISH, and single-molecule imaging).
Through these carefully designed and executed experiments, the authors demonstrate a number of key findings. These include a rather complex mechanism for co-translational assembly formation for this ATP-dependent chaperone system, including identifying mRNA clients involved in co- and post-translational interactions, and the formation of “translation factories”. It is on this latter point which is what is remarkable about this study: the authors present a rather unexpected mechanism of “co-chaperone” channelling, which brings translating mRNA into close proximity into biomolecular condensates, and thus offers a very plausible alternative mechanistic understanding for how protein complexes can be formed. This is significant because the current hypothesis is that complexes form because translating polypeptides are brought into close proximity via polysomes. The specifics of this mechanism are (in my opinion) a little more tenuous and could benefit from more clarification (see below), however overall, there is a very plausible (and exciting) hypothesis that is being put forward.
In summary, this manuscript offers a set of important findings that will attract broad interest across several fields (including protein translation, chaperone interactions, protein folding, and biomolecular condensate formation), and will no doubt inspire related works.
A few considerations that may help to improve the clarity of the manuscript for a broader audience:
1. Puromycin treatment offers a reliable means to detect active translation, however, do the authors detect and ribosomal proteins or rRNA within their proteomic analysis?
2. On a related point, do the authors have evidence for polysome formation or of ribosomal complexes? Polysome formation is of course the default mode by which translation would occur within cells, however some biochemical evidence may provide some unequivocal proof.
3. Within the “translational factories” (cha-cha) mechanism it was not clear to me whether the biomolecular condensates (P-bodies) contained actively translating ribosomes or whether they were simply sequestering mRNA? Often P-bodies are associated with compromises within proteostasis (e.g. regulation), however here the authors suggest a more functional role for localised translation. The authors show that condensates can form from mRNA and local translation is likely to occur. What is missing (or at least not clear to me) is whether there is protein-based evidence that the condensate formation results in assembly formation. This may need to clarify the biomolecular condensate description further to give unequivocal credence to the cha-cha and “translational factories” concepts. I anticipate that the authors are correct, but viewing the mechanism from the lens of mRNA localisation alone might considered limiting.
4. For the non-specialist reader, a description of the significance of the recruitment of POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs would be helpful.

1. Puromycin treatment offers a reliable means to detect active translation, however, do the authors detect any ribosomal proteins or rRNA within their proteomic analysis?
The Reviewer raises an interesting point.
We always detect ribosomal proteins in our R2TP AP-MS experiments. However, they are never above the background noise and therefore can not be considered as specific interactants. Our hypothesis is that there are too few ribosomes bound to R2TP in an ocean of cellular ribosomes, and therefore the R2TP-bound ribosomes do not emerge from the background. We tried to estimate this effect more quantitatively. The estimated number of ribosomes is around 3 000 000 per cell (https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?s=n&v=1&id=107552), while R2TP is moderately expressed. Assuming that the abundance of R2TP is reflected by its mRNA levels, this yields 30 000 copies per cell as the mRNA ratio of RPAP3 vs ribosomal proteins is 0.01. Assuming that 1% of R2TP is bound co-translationally to polysomes, itself having on average ~10 ribosomes, this implies that only 0.1% of ribosomes would interact with R2TP. Even if 10% of R2TP is bound co-translationally to polysomes, it still means that only 1% of ribosomes would interact with R2TP. These numbers are likely beyond the detection threshold. Of note, the search for rRNA in our RUVBL1-GFP and RPAP3-GFP RIP-seq experiments was not possible as rRNAs are systematically depleted during library preparation.
We therefore did two new experiments to detect the interaction of R2TP with ribosomes. First, we generated a RPS6-GFP knock-in cell line and performed smFISH to test whether ribosomes are present in the POLR2A mRNA foci where R2TP also accumulates (Fig. R1 below). Using high resolution confocal imaging, we observed neither an accumulation nor an exclusion of RPS6-GFP from the R2TP-containing POLR2A mRNA foci. This result suggests that ribosomes are present at low levels in the mRNA foci, in agreement with the model that we describe in the manuscript. These new data have been added in the revised manuscript in Fig. S6A.
As a second approach to address the association of R2TP with ribosomes, we performed polysome profiling. We fractionated ribosomes and polysomes on a sucrose gradient and analyzed the presence of RUVBL2 in the different fractions by Western blot (Fig. R2 below). RUVBL2 was detected in fractions 5 to 8, indicating that R2TP is associated with small polysomes in cells. These new data have been added in the revised manuscript (Fig. S2B).
2. On a related point, do the authors have evidence for polysome formation or of ribosomal complexes? Polysome formation is of course the default mode by which translation would occur within cells, however some biochemical evidence may provide some unequivocal proof.
The polysome fractionation experiment of Fig. R2 above provides direct biochemical evidence for an association between R2TP and polysomes. We detect association with light polysomes, but because R2TP associates with only few mRNAs that are moderately expressed, its association with larger polysomes may be beyond our detection limit. Alternatively, the mRNAs associated with R2TP may have only a few ribosomes.
3. Within the “translational factories” (cha-cha) mechanism it was not clear to me whether the biomolecular condensates (P-bodies) contained actively translating ribosomes or whether they were simply sequestering mRNA? Often P-bodies are associated with compromises within proteostasis (e.g. regulation), however here the authors suggest a more functional role for localised translation. The authors show that condensates can form from mRNA and local translation is likely to occur. What is missing (or at least not clear to me) is whether there is protein-based evidence that the condensate formation results in assembly formation. This may need to clarify the biomolecular condensate description further to give unequivocal credence to the cha-cha and “translational factories” concepts. We have now clarified the point concerning the molecular condensates and in particular the issue of P-bodies vs. translation factories. Indeed, we performed experiments with two different types of condensates:
• a first type that is artificially created using a P-body protein fused to a R2TP component.
• a second type that naturally occurs in cells: the POLR2A translation factories.
The artificial condensate forms in the cytoplasm when we use a fragment of a P-body protein: amino-acids 289-483 of DDX6 (referred to as DDX6fm). Indeed, this fragment can be fused to a protein of interest and the resulting fusion protein will artificially accumulate in P-bodies. In the past, we have used this system to look at the co-recruitment of a second protein to these artificial P-bodies, which then provides evidence for an in vivo interaction between the two proteins (see Boulon et al, 2010; Maurizy et al, 2018). In the present manuscript, we adapted the system to look at the recruitment of target mRNAs to the artificial P-bodies. We fused DDX6fm to DsRed2 and either RUVBL1 or RPAP3. RUVBL1 and RPAP3 are not normally present in P-bodies. However, by fusing them to DDX6fm, we artificially concentrate these proteins in P-bodies where they can interact and recruit candidate mRNAs or proteins (Fig.4 and S4 of the revised manuscript). We observed that the artificial concentration of RUVBL1 or RPAP3 in P-bodies leads to the co-recruitment of POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs to these artificial structures, indicating an interaction between the two. Importantly, POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs do not localize to P-bodies in absence of either the DsRed2-DDX6fm-RUVBL1 or the DsRed2-DDX6fm-RPAP3 fusion proteins (see Fig. S6C of the revised manuscript and also below in Fig. R3). Likewise, they are not recruited to the artificial P-bodies formed by DsRed2-DDX6fm-KPNA3, a negative control unrelated to R2TP (Fig. 4 of the revised manuscript).
In the revised manuscript, we clarified the text by adding the sentence: “By fusing them to DDX6fm, we artificially created a high local accumulation of R2TP in P-bodies and could then check by smFISH whether the candidate mRNAs or proteins are recruited into these artificial condensates.”
In contrast to these artificial R2TP condensates, the translation factories are natural endogenous condensates that exist in cells in absence of any treatment, and which concentrate POLR2A mRNA and protein, PRPF8 mRNA and R2TP (Fig. 6 and S6E of the revised manuscript). To avoid any confusion, we performed immunofluorescence experiments to verify that the endogenous POLR2A translation factories are not P-bodies (see Fig. R3 below). As expected, the POLR2A mRNA and protein condensates are distinct from P-bodies. These new data have been added to the revised manuscript (Fig. S6C).
Of note, we believe that actively translating ribosomes are present in both types of condensates, the artificial condensates and the natural POLR2A translation factories. Indeed, for the artificial P-body condensates accumulating R2TP, the POLR2A protein can be detected there together with the POLR2A mRNAs (Fig. 4D of the revised manuscript), and the POLR2A mRNAs dissociate from these artificial R2TP condensates upon translation inhibition (Fig.4A, B and D of the revised manuscript). Likewise, the POLR2A protein is present in the POLR2A translation factories (Figure R3 above and Fig. S6C of the revised manuscript), and these factories are dissolved when translation is inhibited (Fig.6 and S6E of the revised manuscript). Interestingly, this latter effect is observed with puromycin or harringtonine, which dissociate nascent proteins from their mRNAs, but not with cycloheximide, which also inhibits translation but maintains the polysomes intact with the nascent protein chains still attached to the mRNA. This indicates that the nascent POLR2A protein likely plays a key role in driving the assembly of the translation factories (Fig. R4 below, now included in Fig. S7A of the revised manuscript). This is in line with the requirement for HSP90 and R2TP in the formation of the factories (Fig. 8 of the revised manuscript), highlighting a model in which these two chaperones bind their client proteins co-translationally and drive assembly of the factories, possibly because of the multivalency of R2TP (RUVBL1/2 form hexamers and dodecamers) and polysomes (which carry multiple nascent chains).
To further confirm this model, we performed new microscopy experiments showing that the RPS6 ribosomal protein and HSP90 are present in these foci, even though they do not accumulate there (Fig. R1 above and R5 below, corresponding to Fig. S6A and S6B of the revised manuscript).
To better link the POLR2A translation factories with the assembly process, we performed additional experiments using siRNAs against various subunits of the RNA polymerase II. The rationale was to test how a block in assembly, induced by the lack of a subunit, would affect the POLR2A translation factories. The results, shown in Fig. R6 below, indicate that the knock-down of POLR2H, which is nearly always associated with POLR2A during the assembly process (Boulon et al, 2010), leads to the disappearance of the POLR2A mRNA foci. Likewise, the knock-downs of POLR2B or POLR2C, which form another building block of the enzyme (Boulon et al, 2010) also dissolve the POLR2A translation factories. While the mechanisms involved are unclear at this point, they nevertheless reveal a link between the POLR2A translation factories and the presence of its partner subunits, thus revealing a link with the assembly of RNA polymerase II. These new data have not been included in the manuscript because we think that they will be better suited for a future manuscript dedicated to the detailed assembly mechanisms of RNA polymerase II. However, we hope that, together with the dual role of HSP90 and R2TP in the assembly of the enzyme and the formation of the translation factories, these new data will convince the Reviewer that condensate formation is linked to the assembly process.
4. For the non-specialist reader, a description of the significance of the recruitment of POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs would be helpful.
We thank the Reviewer for this suggestion. We have added a small paragraph in the discussion of the revised manuscript to describe the significance of the recruitment of POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs to translation factories, also referred to as “chaperone factories” in the main text:
‘POLR2A and PRPF8 are both large proteins (>210 kDa) that must be assembled into large macromolecular complexes, RNA polymerase II and U5 snRNP, respectively. Even though these two proteins are not part of the same complex, they need to be taken in charge and stabilized by the same chaperone, HSP90/R2TP, as soon as they come out of the ribosome. Indeed, we have previously shown that the cytoplasmic unassembled POLR2A becomes unstable upon HSP90 or R2TP inhibition (Boulon et al, 2010). Likewise, PRPF8 is rapidly degraded in absence of its co-chaperones (Erkelenz et al, 2021). The risk for these large proteins, if they are not properly taken in charge by their chaperones, is that they get misfolded, interact with the wrong partners, aggregate or become unstable. Chaperone factories have a high local concentration of R2TP and may thus favor their co-translational interaction with the chaperone, likely preventing them from these unwanted events. It is unclear why the other mRNAs that also associate with R2TP are absent from the R2TP factories. It may be that POLR2A and PRPF8 have particularities favoring polysome condensation, such as a stronger or higher valency of binding to HSP90 and R2TP, or a controlled ribosomal pausing providing more time for binding the chaperones and condensing the ribosomes.’

We created vectors expressing mCherry-POLR2A or mCherry-EFTUD2 fusions, as well as variants in which a stop codon was inserted immediately after the coding sequences of mCherry. These reporters are thus identical except for the presence of stop codons that prevent the translation of POLR2A or EFTUD2. We stably expressed these reporters in the RUVBL1-GFP knock-in cell line and then analyzed by IP/RT-qPCR whether these mRNAs associate with RUVBL1-GFP. We found that the mCherry-POLR2A and mCherry-EFTUD2 mRNAs associated with RUVBL1-GFP, while the internal stop codon abolished the interaction (Fig. R9 below). This supports the conclusion that the interaction between POLR2A or EFTUD2 mRNAs and RUVBL1-GFP is strictly dependent on the nascent polypeptide. These results have been added to the revised manuscript in Fig. 3E, F.
Altogether, these new results indicate that puromycin is a reliable tool to assess the translation-dependency of interactions and that, for the tested mRNAs, there are no detectable translation-independent interactions between the chaperone and the mRNAs.
3-To further support this possibility, Puromycin treatments seem to have a low impact also in the RPAP3-SUN-TAG experiments (Figure 5), again suggesting translation independent functions. This point needs to be discussed and addressed.
In Fig. 5A of the original manuscript, we use a microscopy assay to show that the proportion of mRNA colocalizing with RPAP3-SunTag significantly decreases upon puromycin treatment, for EP400, EFTUD2, PRPF8 and POLR2A mRNAs. Indeed, as pointed out by the Reviewer, the proportion of co-localizing mRNAs does not go down to 0% in puromycin-treated cells. We believe that this is due to the nature of the assay. Let’s imagine that RPAP3-SunTag occupies 50% of the pixels in a cell, then any spot randomly localized would have a basal colocalization rate of 50% with RPAP3-SunTag. Indeed, we measured that ~15% of 𝛂-catenin mRNA colocalizes with RPAP3-SunTag in both untreated and puromycin-treated cells, although this mRNA is a negative control unrelated to RPAP3, which does not appear in our RIP-Seq experiments. Thus, colocalization values of ~15% represent the baseline.
We believe that the significance of the colocalization is demonstrated by the puromycin treatment and by the comparison with the 𝛂-catenin negative control, rather than by its absolute value. Also, it is important to note that the RPAP3-SunTag protein is expressed at about a 50 fold lower level than the endogenous protein. The true association rate of these mRNAs with RPAP3 is thus likely to be much higher than measured with the RPAP3-SunTag system.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)
This study provides evidence for the co-translational role of the HSP90/R2TP chaperone complex in assembling multi-subunit macromolecular complexes in eukaryotic cells. It proposes an interesting mechanism termed “cha-cha” (co- translational chaperone channeling), whereby R2TP facilitates protein complex assembly not via mRNA co-localization, but through localized condensates — termed R2TP factories — that act as hubs for translation and assembly. These factories accumulate client mRNAs and facilitate efficient subunit interaction via chaperone mediation.
I have some doubts about the validity of the conclusions:
Strictly speaking, RIP-seq and FISH just shows that the tagged protein binds RNA species in a more or less specific manner.
1-The conclusion that this is co-translational is not fully substantiated. Given that puromycin only reduces (some of) the mRNAs association, that would require additional controls, like showing ribosomal proteins and RNA are co-precipitated. Ribosome profiling or ribosome-nascent chain complex IP would lend further credibility.
This is an interesting point that is also raised by Reviewer 1. As mentioned in the response to Reviewer 1 (see his/her point 1), we have tried to detect an interaction between R2TP and ribosomal proteins by different means (AP-MS and IF). In summary, there are only a few ribosomes bound to R2TP, which are diluted in an ocean of other cellular ribosomes, and therefore the background will be very high in any kind of interaction assay using R2TP as bait, and will preclude detection. We thus performed a series of alternative experiments to rigorously demonstrate the co-translational nature of the interactions detected by RIP-seq.
-As mentioned above in our response to Reviewer 1, we have now performed polysome profiling experiments and analyzed the presence of RUVBL2 in the different polysomal fractions. We found that RUVBL2 is present in small amounts in light polysome fractions (Fig. R2 above).
-As suggested by the Reviewer, we have also performed an experiment inspired from the RiboSeq-nascent chain IP method. In this experiment, we immunoprecipitated RUVBL1-GFP from cell extracts and treated the beads with a saturating amount of RNAse I to degrade all the free pieces of RNA and keep only the ribosome protected fragments associated with RUVBL1-GFP. Completion of RNA degradation was ensured by spiking an in vitro translated RNA directly on the IP’ed beads and verifying by gel that it was degraded to pieces of <10 nucleotides. The protected RNA fragments were then sequenced. Below in Fig. R10, we provide browser tracks for POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs, the main R2TP mRNA targets, along with two abundant control mRNAs that do not associate with R2TP in the RIP-Seq experiments, EEF1D and EEF1G. We observed that many reads are distributed along the coding sequence of the POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNA, while very few are present on the 5’ and 3’ UTR regions of these mRNAs, or on the control mRNA that does not bind R2TP (Fig. R10A). Moreover, the reads sizes show two peaks of 32 and 38 nucleotides, suggesting that we predominantly detect single ribosome footprints. Interestingly, the reads start near the N-terminus of PRPF8, while they pile-up in the long last exon of POLR2A, suggesting that the timing of R2TP co-translational recruitment is different for these two mRNAs: early during translation for PRPF8, and late for POLR2A.
Because the manuscript is already heavy in data and because we would also like to optimize this experiment to obtain more read counts and better define the timing of R2TP co-translational recruitment, these new data have not been incorporated in the revised manuscript. Nevertheless, the results confirm the co-translational nature of the recruitment of RUVBL1 on POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs.
-We developed reporters enabling a direct assessment of the co-translational nature of the interactions made by RUVBL1. As shown in the response to Reviewer 2 and in Fig. R9 above, we created reporter cell lines stably expressing mCherry-POLR2A and mCherry-EFTUD2 fusions, with or without a stop codon immediately after the mCherry coding sequences. We found that mCherry-POLR2A and mCherry-EFTUD2 mRNAs nicely associated with RUVBL1-GFP, while the mCherry-STOP-POLR2A and mCherry-STOP-EFTUD2 mRNAs did not (Fig. R9 above). These mRNAs are identical except for the stop codon, and these results thus provide strong support to our conclusion that the interaction between POLR2A or EFTUD2 mRNAs and RUVBL1-GFP is co-translational and depends on the nascent polypeptide. These results have been added to the manuscript in Fig. 3E and F.
-Regarding the point raised by Reviewer 3 that puromycin only reduces RUVBL1 association with some of the mRNAs, we show below in Fig. R11 the RPKM counts of the most interesting mRNAs in the GFP and the control IP. Of note, puromycin reduces binding of RUVBL1-GFP to these mRNAs to a level similar to the control IP, indicating that there is little or no interaction in absence of translation. We do agree that it is possible that some mRNAs species may associate with RUVBL1-GFP independently of translation, but this is clearly not the case for the main hits found in the RIP-Seq experiments. Also, please note that such putative translation-independent mRNA targets are beyond the scope of the present study.
2-Also, Puromycin acts fast and globally. Using translation initiation inhibitors (like harringtonine) would confirm that effects are not due to general ribosome collapse.
We thank the Reviewer for this advice. We have now performed RUVBL1-GFP IPs followed by RTqPCR to compare the effects of puromycin, cycloheximide and harringtonine. The results are presented in Fig. R7 above. In brief, puromycin and harringtonine, two translation inhibitors that dissociate nascent chains from polysomes, abolish the association of RUVBL1-GFP with POLR2A, POLR2B, EFTUD2, PRPF8, EP400 and BRD8 mRNAs, whereas cycloheximide, a translation inhibitor that freezes ribosomes and stabilizes polysomes, slightly increases it. These results indicate that the nascent protein chain must remain associated with the mRNA to enable RUVBL1 binding. These results have been added to Fig. 3D of the manuscript.
3-The claim that mRNAs were found that code for proteins that assemble into complexes needs statistical testing to see if this is above what you would randomly expect to find from pulling down that many mRNAs, in particular for related proteins it could just be based on sequence or property similarity.
We do not claim that the RIP-Seq experiments show by themselves a role of R2TP in client assembly. We only observed that most mRNAs found in the RIP-Seq experiments code for proteins that are known to be assembled together by R2TP. In particular, this was previously shown for RNA polymerase II (Boulon et al, 2010; Forget et al, 2013; Lynham and Houry, 2022) and U5 snRNP (Malinova et al, 2017; Cloutier et al, 2017). The text was clarified.
4-The CB-6644 drug specificity is unclear to me. Complementing knockout/ knockdown with ATPase-dead mutants would solidify ATP-dependence interpretations.
RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 are essential genes. Therefore, knockout cannot be used to answer this question and developing degrons has proved to be unsuccessful so far as well. RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 ATPase-dead mutants show a significant decrease in the ATPase activity of the RUVBL1/2 heterohexamer in vitro (up to 80% activity inhibition with only one mutant in the complex and 90% when both mutants are combined; Assimon et al, 2019). However, previous studies in yeast have shown that these mutants are very toxic and thus would be very difficult to use in the mammalian system (King et al., 2001). Importantly, the drug CB-6644 shows an inhibition of ~80% of RUVBL1/2 ATPase activity in vitro, and displays a similar effect as the ATPase-dead mutants (Garcia-Martin et al, 2024). In addition, CB-6644 has been considered selective for RUVBL1/2, since it does not have any activity on related AAA ATPases (Assimon et al, 2019), and furthermore, while CB-6644 inhibits cell growth, these effects can be reverted by a single point mutant of the RUVBLs that prevents CB-6644 binding (Assimon et al, 2019).
The mechanism of action of the drug has now been well described, thanks to recent cryo-EM studies (Garcia-Martin et al, 2024). It was shown that CB-6644 recognizes the ATP-bound conformation of the RUVBL1/2 heterohexamer by interacting at the interface between two RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunits, thereby trapping the ATP-bound conformation of the complex and preventing ATP hydrolysis (Garcia-Martin et al, 2024). Importantly, the drug CB-6644 inhibits the activity of the RUVBL1/2 complex but not the activity of each individual protein. Therefore we are confident that the drug CB-6644 is a powerful tool to specifically and rapidly inhibit RUVBL1/2 activity in cells. Given the toxicity of the ATPase dead mutants of the RUVBLs, it would be very difficult to devise a suitable expression system to perform RIP-seq experiments with them, and results may also be prone to artefacts.
5-For the RNAs that are seen to remain associated with R2TP in the absence of translation (by addition of puromycin), the authors could stain for ribosomal proteins, to see if entire ribosome nascent chain complexes are attached to R2TP.
This is an interesting point. Indeed, translation-independent mRNAs may in fact still be interacting via the nascent chain if the ribosomes are stuck in long pauses. We feel that this could be the topic of future studies since the present manuscript is focused on the co-translational recruitment of the HSP90/R2TP chaperone by certain clients.
We have performed microscopy experiments to test the colocalization of RPS6-GFP ribosomal protein with POLR2A mRNA. As for proteins interacting both co- and post-translationally with the R2TP chaperone, we observed that for POLR2A and PRPF8, the peptides identified by AP-MS experiments are located along the entire length of these proteins (see Fig. R12 below). Likewise, peptide intensity is relatively homogeneous along the POLR2A and PRPF8 proteins and we do not see an enrichment at their N-termini (Fig. R12C).

7-The control condition of the RIP-seq is poorly chosen, the GFP-trap beads have single-chain antibody against GFP, the authors use as a control just naked agarose beads. At the very least this should be an off-target nanobody and preferably, the experiment should also have been done with the GFP-trap beads in cells where the target is not tagged.
We thank the Reviewer for pointing this out. Each type of IP internal control has its advantages and disadvantages and it is indeed better to perform both. The use of naked agarose beads with RUVBL1-GFP extracts allowed us to bypass the proteome variations that could be due to clonal variation between cell lines. Conversely, using GFP-TRAP beads with the parental cells would allow us to bypass the risk that naked agarose beads do not bind exactly the same contaminants as the GFP-TRAP beads.
We have thus performed new RUVBL1-GFP IP/RT-qPCR experiments to test different types of internal controls, i.e., parental cells with GFP-TRAP beads (IP-GFP HCT116-WT), RUVBL1-GFP cells with FLAG beads (IP-FLAG HCT116-RUVBL1-GFP) and RUVBL1-GFP cells with naked agarose beads (IP-CTL HCT116-RUVBL1-GFP). The results are presented in Fig. R13 below and show that all three controls are similar. In addition, we can confirm interactions of RUVBL1-GFP with the mRNAs coding for POLR2A, POLRB, EFTUD2, PRPF8, EP400 and BRD8, while POLR2C and POLR2H are not enriched in the GFP IPs as compared to the controls.
8- In the context of co-translational events, the ribosome is a key player. It’s noteworthy that the authors discuss co-translational processes and interactions without discussing/addressing ribosomal RNA or ribosomal proteins throughout the paper. I suggest using an antibody against a ribosomal protein to stain HeLa cells and look for signals in the foci discussed. Additionally, if applicable, mention that in the label-free proteomics, ribosomal proteins were found in the IP which disappeared when treated with puromycin. This confirms that when the NCs are released, the rRNA and ribosomal proteins should also be reduced significantly. Furthermore, additional western blots should be conducted to verify and confirm the presence of ribosomes in the IP pulldown step with anti-GFP beads.
This is similar to the points 1 and 5 of the Reviewer 1.
As mentioned above (see point 1 of Reviewer 1), there are only a few ribosomes bound to R2TP, which are diluted in a vast amount of non-interacting ribosomes. These non-interacting ribosomes generate background and detecting an enrichment of ribosomes in a R2TP IP is thus extremely difficult if not impossible.
Likewise, ribosomes are present throughout the entire cytoplasm with a concentration of ~1 𝜇M (https://tinyurl.com/vkav59yb), it is therefore very difficult to detect any enrichment of ribosomes on single mRNAs (see example images in Fig. R1).
However, as discussed above, we have now performed a series of experiments rigorously demonstrating the co-translational nature of the interaction of R2TP with its target mRNAs:
• Polysome profiling experiments show the presence of RUVBL2 in light polysome fractions (Fig. R2 above).
• Experiments inspired from the IP/RiboSeq method showed that we can detect ribosome protected-fragments in RUVBL1-GFP IPs, which are located along the POLR2A and PRPF8 mRNAs but not control mRNAs (Fig. R10 above).
• The use of multiple translation inhibitors (puromycin, harringtonine and cycloheximide), demonstrate that the nascent polypeptide is essential to promote the association of RUVBL1 with its target mRNAs.
• The use of mCherry fusion reporters bearing or not a stop codon in between the mCherry and POLR2A (or EFTUD2), demonstrates that the POLR2A and EFTUD2 RNA sequences must be translated to promote association with RUVBL1 (Fig. R9 above).
Altogether, we believe that these new results demonstrate beyond doubt that RUVBL1 interacts with its main mRNA targets via the nascent protein chains.

We would like to point out that most proteins identified in our AP-MS experiments were previously shown to interact with RUVBL1/2 (Maurizy et al. 2018, Cloutier et al. 2017, Rizzolo et al. 2017, Cho el al. 2021). Therefore, we believe that it was not necessary to confirm those interactions by WB.
